sections.h2: What should a seller know about Piscataway before listing?
sections.html:
Piscataway will not let a home change occupants without a Municipal Certificate of Continued Compliance. The requirement has applied to sales and rentals since January 1, 2019, and it is the step that most often sets the calendar for a closing.

The township covers 18.79 square miles of Middlesex County and had an estimated 62,253 residents on July 1, 2025, up 2.4 percent from the 2020 base. Values run well above the national figure of $332,700: the median owner-occupied home is $449,900, median gross rent is $2,024 and median household income is $127,832. Owners live in 63.8 percent of homes, across 17,664 households. Rutgers University's Busch and Livingston campuses lie inside the township, which keeps demand steady. Neighborhoods such as Arbor, Johnson Park, Lake Nelson, New Market, North Stelton, Riverview Manor and Society Hill appear in listings, so use the one buyers recognize.

sections.h2: How the Piscataway MCCC inspection works
sections.html:
The Community Development Department inspects each dwelling for fitness for habitation and issues the certificate if it passes. Inspections take place weekdays from 8 a.m. to noon and 1:30 to 3:30 p.m., excluding holidays, and inspectors show a township vehicle and photo identification at the door.

The township asks sellers to apply at least four weeks before closing. Applications and fees go to the MCCC office at the Public Works Center, reachable at (732) 562-2393 or mccc@piscatawaynj.org. Section 14-4 of the municipal code governs the program.

Piscataway MCCC fees
Certificate typeFee
Single-family home, condo or townhome$150 per unit
Two-family$300 in total
Temporary MCCC, after an application is filed$125 per unit
Reinspection, starting with the third inspection$100 per unit

One rule catches many sellers: if work was done without a required permit, the permit must be obtained and any open permits closed before the certificate is issued. Dig out old deck, basement and kitchen permits early.

sections.h2: Getting a Piscataway house ready for the MCCC
sections.html:
Preparation starts with paperwork, because unpermitted work holds up the certificate. The partial checklist on the township site is a guide to what homes most commonly fail, and it is not a full list of every possible reason.

  • Submit the application and fee at least four weeks before the closing date.
  • Walk the house with a permit list in hand and note anything built or replaced since you bought it. Collect permits for decks, finished basements, additions, water heaters and electrical work, and close any that are still open.
  • Plan the visit for a weekday window, and expect inspectors to show photo identification.
  • Budget for the third inspection onward, which costs $100 per unit.
  • Ask whether a temporary certificate fits your timeline if repairs will run past closing.

Older housing stock is part of the picture. The Road Up Raritan Historic District holds nine historic homes along River Road, and a house dating to 1741 operates as a county museum. Owners in or near historic areas should ask the Planning Division what local review applies before promising a buyer exterior changes.

sections.h2: Property taxes when you sell in Piscataway
sections.html:
Ask the township Tax Collector for a current statement before you set a closing date, because balances and installments change through the year. The tax office also publishes the township's rates.

In April 2026 the township announced a budget that lowered the municipal tax rate by another 4.72 percent to offset gains in property value. A lower rate does not guarantee a lower bill, since assessed values and county and school levies move too, so compare your own bill line by line.

Taxes and sewer charges can be paid online through the township website, which helps when a title company needs proof that accounts are current.

sections.h2: Who records the deed for a Piscataway sale?
sections.html:
The Middlesex County Clerk's registry in New Brunswick records deeds for Piscataway properties. The office opens weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4:10 p.m. and asks walk-in filers to arrive by 4 p.m.; appointments are optional but get priority.

A deed must say "Prepared by" and name the drafter, show the tax block, lot and consideration, and give a record-and-return address. Signatures must be original with the names printed beneath. A re-recorded deed needs a new affidavit, a new seller's residency form and a new cover sheet. Title companies commonly file electronically through the New Jersey County Recording system instead.

State forms go with the deed. Married sellers who file a joint state return may sign one Gross Income Tax form, while unmarried co-owners each sign their own, matched to their ownership share. A nonresident seller prepays at least 2 percent of the sale price. Heirs selling an inherited house sign the form that fits their own residency. The seller also pays the state realty transfer fee at recording.

sections.h2: A step-by-step plan for a Piscataway closing
sections.html:
Work from the closing date backward. At least four weeks out, file the MCCC application with the Public Works Center office and pay the fee. Before that, collect every permit for past work and close the open ones, since that rule applies to any house.

Plan for the inspection window on a weekday, remembering that inspectors work mornings and early afternoons only, with an adult available to let the inspector in. If the house fails, fix the items and book the reinspection. Reinspection fees start with the third inspection, at $100 per unit. Should repairs run past your closing date, ask about the $125 temporary certificate once the application is filed.

In the final weeks, request the tax statement, confirm the deed details with your attorney or title company, and decide who signs which Gross Income Tax form. Keep copies of the certificate and any closed permits, since a buyer's lender or attorney may ask for them.

sections.h2: Is a cash sale worth considering in Piscataway?
sections.html:
It can be, when a house is likely to fail the MCCC inspection, has open permits or has sat vacant. A cash buyer may accept the property without the repairs a seller would otherwise fund, but the certificate still comes before any change of occupancy, and the township also offers a temporary version at $125 per unit once an application is filed.

Call the MCCC office before you sign to confirm the process for your address. Ask any buyer who files the MCCC application, who pays the fees, and what happens if reinspections run past the second visit. Because the certificate must be in hand before anyone moves in, a buyer who plans to rent the house needs one too. Weigh the offer against what you would net after repairs, the seller's transfer fee and the months a listing may take.

faqs.q: Does Piscataway require an inspection to sell a house?
faqs.a: Yes. A Municipal Certificate of Continued Compliance is required when selling or renting a home, and the township asks for the application four weeks before closing.

faqs.q: How much does a Piscataway MCCC cost?
faqs.a: It costs $150 per unit for a single-family home, condo or townhome, $300 for a two-family, and $125 per unit for a temporary certificate. Reinspections cost $100 per unit starting with the third.

faqs.q: What happens if I did work in Piscataway without a permit?
faqs.a: The permit must be obtained and any open permits closed before the certificate is issued. Start that step early because it can hold up a closing.

faqs.q: Where is the Piscataway MCCC office?
faqs.a: It operates from the Public Works Center. Call (732) 562-2393 or email mccc@piscatawaynj.org for an appointment.
At the Middlesex County Clerk's registry at 75 Bayard Street in New Brunswick, or electronically through the county's e-recording service for title companies.
